subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Weather and Climate
subtitle: Reading practice for KS3 weather, climate and climate change.
description: Reading passages and comprehension questions based on the KS3 Weather and Climate source pack. Passages practise retrieval, inference, data use and explanation using weather and climate vocabulary.

data.sourcePassage: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere over a short time, such as a day or a week. Climate is the average pattern of weather over a much longer period, usually at least 30 years. This difference matters because one hot day, storm or snowy morning is not enough to prove a climate trend. Geographers measure weather with instruments such as thermometers, rain gauges, anemometers, wind vanes and barometers. To make data reliable, instruments should be used in the same way each time and placed carefully. A thermometer beside a sunny brick wall may record air that is too warm, while a rain gauge under a tree may collect too little rainfall. Good fieldwork uses fair sites, clear units and repeated measurements.

questions.question: How long is usually used to calculate climate averages?
questions.modelAnswer: Climate averages are usually calculated over at least 30 years.

questions.question: Which instrument measures air pressure?
questions.modelAnswer: A barometer measures air pressure.

questions.question: Why is one storm not enough to prove climate change?
questions.modelAnswer: One storm is a short-term weather event, while climate change is identified using long-term patterns across many years.

questions.question: Why should weather instruments be placed away from buildings and trees?
questions.modelAnswer: Buildings and trees can affect readings by creating shade, blocking wind, adding heat or reducing rainfall reaching a gauge.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.modelAnswer: Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge in millimetres.

data.sourcePassage: Most rainfall begins with rising air. Water evaporates from seas, lakes, rivers and soil, adding water vapour to the air. When air rises, it cools. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapour, so condensation forms tiny water droplets. These droplets make clouds and can eventually join together to fall as precipitation. At KS3, three rainfall types are especially important. Relief rainfall happens when moist air is forced over high land, which is common in western parts of the UK. Convectional rainfall begins when strong sunshine heats the ground and warm air rises, often creating heavy showers. Frontal rainfall happens when warm air meets colder, denser air and is forced to rise over it.

questions.question: What happens to air as it rises?
questions.modelAnswer: As air rises, it cools.

questions.question: Which rainfall type is caused by moist air rising over high land?
questions.modelAnswer: Relief rainfall is caused by moist air rising over high land.

questions.question: Explain why condensation is important in rainfall formation.
questions.modelAnswer: Condensation changes cooled water vapour into droplets, which form clouds and can grow into precipitation.

questions.question: How is convectional rainfall different from frontal rainfall?
questions.modelAnswer: Convectional rainfall starts when heated ground makes warm air rise, while frontal rainfall happens when warm air is forced over colder air at a front.

questions.question: Why is relief rainfall common in parts of western UK?
questions.modelAnswer: Moist Atlantic air carried by prevailing winds is forced to rise over western uplands, cools and condenses.

data.sourcePassage: The UK has changeable weather because it is influenced by different air masses, pressure systems and the surrounding sea. Maritime air has travelled over the sea, so it is usually moist. Continental air has travelled over land, so it is often drier. Tropical air tends to be warmer, while polar or Arctic air is colder. The UK can receive tropical maritime, polar maritime, tropical continental, polar continental and Arctic maritime air at different times. Pressure systems also matter. High pressure usually has sinking air and settled weather. Low pressure has rising air, cloud, rain and often stronger winds. The west of the UK is generally wetter than the east because south-westerly winds bring moist Atlantic air towards western uplands, where relief rainfall forms.

questions.question: What does maritime air mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Maritime air is air that has travelled over the sea.

questions.question: Which pressure system is most linked to rising air, cloud and rain?
questions.modelAnswer: Low pressure is linked to rising air, cloud and rain.

questions.question: Why is the west of the UK generally wetter than the east?
questions.modelAnswer: Prevailing south-westerly winds bring moist Atlantic air to western uplands, where air rises, cools and produces relief rainfall.

questions.question: How can high pressure produce different weather in summer and winter?
questions.modelAnswer: In summer, settled clear skies can bring sunny hot weather, but in winter clear skies can allow heat to escape, causing frost or fog.

questions.question: Name two reasons the UK weather changes often.
questions.modelAnswer: The UK is affected by different air masses and pressure systems, and it is surrounded by sea.

data.sourcePassage: Climate varies around the world because places receive different amounts of heat and moisture. Latitude is important because the Sun rays are more direct near the Equator and more spread out near the poles. Altitude also matters because higher places are usually colder. Distance from the sea affects temperature range: coastal areas often have milder winters and cooler summers than inland areas. Ocean currents, prevailing winds and relief can also change temperature and rainfall. These controls help create climate zones such as tropical rainforest, hot desert, temperate maritime, Mediterranean, polar and mountain climates. Geographers often use climate graphs to compare places. Bars usually show rainfall in millimetres and a line usually shows temperature in degrees Celsius. Strong descriptions quote figures rather than saying only hot, cold, wet or dry.

questions.question: What does latitude measure?
questions.modelAnswer: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator.

questions.question: On most climate graphs, rainfall is shown by what?
questions.modelAnswer: Rainfall is usually shown by bars.

questions.question: Explain why places near the Equator are usually warmer than places near the poles.
questions.modelAnswer: Near the Equator, the Sun rays are more direct and concentrated, while near the poles they are spread over a larger area.

questions.question: Why should climate graph answers include data?
questions.modelAnswer: Data makes the description precise and supports claims about temperature and rainfall patterns.

questions.question: Give two climate controls other than latitude.
questions.modelAnswer: Altitude, distance from sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds and relief are climate controls.

data.sourceTitle: Extreme Weather and Climate Change Responses
data.targetTitle: Extreme Weather and Climate Change Responses
data.sourcePassage: Extreme weather is weather that is unusual, severe or dangerous for a place. In the UK, heatwaves can cause dehydration, increase water demand, damage transport surfaces and make wildfires more likely during dry periods. Flooding can damage homes and businesses, close roads and railways, contaminate water and increase repair costs. Climate change may increase some risks, but geographers must use long-term evidence rather than one event. Evidence includes rising global average temperatures, melting glaciers, shrinking Arctic sea ice, sea-level rise and changing rainfall patterns. Responses can be grouped as mitigation or adaptation. Mitigation reduces the causes of climate change, for example renewable energy or better public transport. Adaptation helps people cope with impacts, for example flood defences, heatwave plans and drought-resistant crops.

questions.question: What does mitigation mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Mitigation means reducing the causes of climate change.

questions.question: Which option is an adaptation strategy?
questions.modelAnswer: Flood defences are an adaptation strategy because they reduce damage from flooding.

questions.question: Explain one social impact of a UK heatwave.
questions.modelAnswer: A heatwave can cause dehydration or heat illness, especially for older people or people in built-up areas.

questions.question: Why do geographers use long-term evidence when studying climate change?
questions.modelAnswer: Climate change is about long-term patterns, so evidence across many years is more reliable than one extreme event.

questions.question: Give two pieces of evidence for climate change named in the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Evidence includes rising global temperatures, melting glaciers, shrinking Arctic sea ice, sea-level rise and changing rainfall patterns.
